--- title: "Multivariate Linear Regression" description: "Extending linear regression to model a continuous outcome using multiple predictor variables." image: "Figures/multiple_regression_3D.gif" categories: [Regression] order: 2 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles To study relationships between multiple continuous independent variables (e.g., the effect of weight and age on height), we can use a multiple regression approach. Essentially, we extend [Linear Regression for continuous variable](1. Linear Regression for continuous variable.qmd) by adding a regression coefficient $\beta_x$ for each continuous variable (e.g., $\beta_{weight}$ and $\beta_{age}$). ## Considerations ::: callout-note - We have the same considerations as for the [Regression for continuous variable](1. Linear Regression for continuous variable.qmd). - The model interpretation of the regression coefficients $\beta_x$ is considered for fixed values of the other independent variable(s)' regression coefficients—i.e., for a given age, $\beta_{weight}$ represents the expected change in the dependent variable (height) for each one-unit increase in weight, holding all other variables (e.g., age) constant. ::: ## Example Below is example code demonstrating Bayesian multiple linear regression using the BayesForge (BF) package. Data consist of three continuous variables (*height*, *weight*, *age*), and the goal is to estimate the effect of *weight* and *age* on *height*. This example is based on @mcelreath2018statistical. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {#ea8a4e86 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform='cpu') # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ from importlib.resources import files # Import data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path = True) m.data(data_path, sep=';') m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] # Subset data to adults m.scale(['weight', 'age']) # Normalize # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(height, weight, age): # Parameter prior distributions alpha = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = 'alpha') beta1 = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = 'beta1') beta2 = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = 'beta2') sigma = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = 'sigma') # Likelihood m.dist.normal(alpha + beta1 * weight + beta2 * age, sigma, obs = height) # Run MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. Subset data to adults m$scale(list('weight', 'age')) # Normalize m$data_to_model(list('weight', 'height', 'age')) # Send to model (convert to jax array) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(height, weight, age){ # Parameter prior distributions alpha = bf.dist.normal(178, 20, name = 'alpha') beta1 = bf.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = 'beta1') beta2 = bf.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = 'beta2') sigma = bf.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = 'sigma') # Likelihood bf.dist.normal(alpha + beta1 * weight + beta2 * age, sigma, obs=height) } # Run MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m$summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ### Julia ```Julia using PyBayesForge # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ # Import data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep=';') m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] # Subset data to adults m.scale(["weight", "age"]) # Normalize # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(height, weight, age) # Parameter prior distributions alpha = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "alpha") beta1 = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = "beta1") beta2 = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, name = "beta2") sigma = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "sigma") # Likelihood m.dist.normal(alpha + beta1 * weight + beta2 * age, sigma, obs = height) end # Run mcmc ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ::: ::: callout-caution For R users, if you create the regression coefficient in a single call: ```{.r .no-test .lang-only} betas = m$dist$normal(0, 0.5, name = 'regression_coefficients', shape = c(2)) ``` you need to index them starting by 0: ```{.r .no-test .lang-only} m$dist$normal(alpha + betas[0] * weight + betas[1] * age, sigma, obs = height) ``` ::: ## Mathematical Details ### *Frequentist formulation* We model the relationship between the independent variables $(X_{1i}, X_{2i}, ..., X_{[K,i]})$ and the dependent variable _Y_ using the following equation: $$ 𝑌_i = \alpha +\beta_1 𝑋_{[1,i]} + \beta_2 𝑋_{[2,i]} + ... + \beta_n 𝑋_{[K,i]} + \epsilon_i $$ Where: - $Y_i$ is the dependent variable for observation *i*. - $\alpha$ is the intercept term. - $X_{[1,i]}$, $X_{[2,i]}$, ..., $X_{[K,i]}$ are the values of the independent variables for observation *i*. - $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, ..., $\beta_K$ are the regression coefficients. - $\epsilon_i$ is the error term for observation *i*, and the vector of the error terms, $\epsilon$, are assumed to be independent and identically distributed. ### *Bayesian formulation* In the Bayesian formulation, we define each parameter with [priors 🛈]{#prior}. We can express the Bayesian model as follows: $$ 𝑌_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_k X_{[K,i]}, σ) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(178, 20) $$ $$ \beta_k \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) $$ $$ σ \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ Where: - $Y_i$ is the dependent variable for observation *i*. - $\alpha$ is the intercept term, with a Normal(178, 20) prior centred on a plausible adult height (height is not scaled). - $\beta_k$ are slope coefficients for the _K_ distinct independent variables, with Normal(0, 0.5) priors (the predictors are scaled). - $X_{[1,i]}$, $X_{[2,i]}$, ..., $X_{[K,i]}$ are the values of the independent variables for observation *i*. - $\sigma$ is a standard deviation parameter, which here has a Uniform prior that constrains it to be positive. ## Model validation tests - [Comparison with Stan](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/blob/main/Test/4.%20Rethinking/Numpyro%20backend/1b.Multiple%20continuous%20variables.py): `1b.Multiple continuous variables.py` fits the same model with BayesForge and Stan and compares the posterior distributions (KL divergence) and parameter recovery. - [Data generative model and inference model pipeline](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/blob/main/Test/4.%20Rethinking/Numpyro%20backend/1b.Multiple%20continuous%20variables.py): `1b.Multiple continuous variables.py` simulates data from the model with known parameters (data generative model), fits the inference model to each simulated dataset and checks that the parameters are recovered. - [Documentation examples (Python)](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation/Python): the Python examples of this page are run by `test_model_pages.py`. - [Documentation examples (R)](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation/R): the R examples of this page are run by `test_r_model_pages.py`. - [Documentation examples (Julia)](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation/Julia): the Julia examples of this page are run by `test_julia_model_pages.py`. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Plot: comparison with Stan (`1b.Multiple continuous variables.py`) ![](Figures/validation/1b.Multiple_continuous_variables_comparison.png){width=100%} ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Plot: data generative model and inference model pipeline (`1b.Multiple continuous variables.py`) ![](Figures/validation/1b.Multiple_continuous_variables_recovery.png){width=100%} ::: ## Reference(s) ::: {#refs} :::
